Rationale: the exclusionary rule deters police misconduct — excluding evidence does not deter judges/magistrates who issued defective warrants; the officer who relied in good faith derived no benefit from the constitutional violation and would not be deterred by exclusion. Four situations where good faith does NOT apply (Leon exceptions): (1) The issuing magistrate/judge was misled by affiant who provided deliberately false or recklessly misleading information (Franks situation); (2) The issuing magistrate wholly abandoned the judicial role (rubber-stamping affidavits without review); (3) The underlying affidavit was so lacking in probable cause as to render any professional officer's reliance on it unreasonable ('bare bones' affidavit); (4) The warrant was facially deficient — so lacking particularity in describing the place or items to be seized that the officer could not reasonably presume it valid. Herring v. United States (2009): expanded Leon beyond warrant cases. Police arrested Herring based on a database entry showing an outstanding warrant that had actually been recalled. Herring argued the arrest was unlawful (no valid warrant). Roberts held: exclusion is not automatic; the critical question is whether the constitutional violation was the result of deliberate, reckless, or grossly negligent police conduct — or isolated, attenuated, or recurring negligence. Police negligence in maintaining warrant databases does not trigger exclusion if it was not systemic and deliberate. This extended good faith beyond the warrant context to situations of police record-keeping error.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe Leon's general holding but will omit one or more of the four specific exceptions where good faith cannot apply, and will not address Herring's extension of good faith to non-warrant negligent police errors

question: Explain the constitutional framework for eyewitness identification procedures, including the due process reliability test from Neil v. Biggers, the Stovall v. Denno suggestiveness analysis, and the significance of Perry v. New Hampshire in limiting suppression rights.
ground_truth: Constitutional framework for eyewitness identifications rests on the Due Process Clause (not the Fourth Amendment or right to counsel, which are separate). Stovall v. Denno (1967): the analysis begins with whether law enforcement used unnecessarily suggestive identification procedures. Unnecessary suggestiveness: a procedure is unnecessarily suggestive if it emphasises the suspect (single-person show-up, telling the witness the suspect is present in the lineup, filling a photo array with dissimilar foils). Neil v. Biggers (1972): even if the procedure was unnecessarily suggestive, suppression is not automatic. The court applies a totality-of-circumstances reliability analysis to determine whether the identification is sufficiently reliable to be admitted despite suggestiveness. Biggers factors: (1) Opportunity of witness to view the suspect; (2) Witness's degree of attention; (3) Accuracy of witness's prior description; (4) Level of certainty at time of confrontation; (5) Time elapsed between crime and identification. If reliability outweighs suggestiveness, the identification is admissible and credibility is for the jury. Perry v. New Hampshire (2012): significantly limited the Due Process framework. The Court held that the constitutional reliability analysis (Biggers) applies ONLY when law enforcement arranged the suggestive circumstances. If suggestiveness arose from circumstances outside police control (e.g., the witness spontaneously identified the defendant standing next to a police car), no due process reliability hearing is required — the identification is admissible and defendant's remedy is cross-examination and expert testimony. This left many unreliable identifications beyond constitutional suppression reach.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the Biggers reliability factors but will not identify the Perry v. New Hampshire limitation that constrains the entire framework to police-arranged suggestiveness, excluding the majority of real-world unreliable identification scenarios

question: What is the inevitable discovery exception in criminal procedure, and how did the Supreme Court in Nix v. Williams hold that it differs from harmless error analysis? What must the prosecution prove and to what standard?
ground_truth: Inevitable discovery doctrine (Nix v. Williams, 1984): even if evidence was discovered through a constitutional violation, it may be admitted if the prosecution proves that the evidence inevitably would have been discovered through independent, lawful means already being employed or that would have been employed had the illegality not occurred. Nix v. Williams facts: police, in violation of Brewer v. Williams' right-to-counsel ruling, elicited incriminating statements leading to a body. At the time, hundreds of searchers were systematically searching the area and would have found the body independently. Court's holding: inevitable discovery is a valid exception to the exclusionary rule because the same deterrence rationale governs — if the evidence would have been found lawfully, exclusion provides no deterrent benefit but substantial social cost. Standard of proof: the prosecution must establish by a preponderance of evidence that the lawful discovery was inevitable. Distinction from harmless error (Chapman v. California): harmless error analysis applies after a constitutional violation has already been established and asks whether the error contributed to the verdict. The standard is beyond a reasonable doubt. Inevitable discovery asks whether the evidence should be admitted at all — it is a threshold admissibility question about whether the evidence is 'tainted' in a meaningful sense. The two doctrines operate at different stages and with different standards. Nix rejected a higher-than-preponderance standard for inevitable discovery, reasoning that requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt would essentially eliminate the doctrine since inevitability by definition involves some uncertainty.
expected_failure: ADMF will conflate inevitable discovery with harmless error, applying the 'beyond reasonable doubt' standard (correct for harmless error) to inevitable discovery rather than the preponderance of evidence standard that Nix established

question: Under FRE 404(b), when is evidence of prior bad acts admissible and what are the procedural requirements? Distinguish between the majority and minority approaches to the 'inclusion' vs. 'exclusion' framing of the rule.
ground_truth: FRE 404(b)(1): evidence of a crime, wrong, or other act is not admissible to prove a person's character in order to show that on a particular occasion the person acted in conformity with that character. 404(b)(2): but evidence is admissible for another purpose — including proof of motive, opportunity, intent, preparation, plan, knowledge, identity, absence of mistake, or lack of accident. The list is non-exhaustive ('may be admissible'). Procedural requirements (2011 amendments): (1) Prosecution must provide reasonable notice to the defendant in criminal cases of its intent to offer 404(b) evidence — advance notice in writing with the general nature of the act; (2) Court must apply Rule 403 balancing: even if the evidence has a permissible purpose, it must be excluded if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the danger of unfair prejudice. Limiting instruction required if defendant requests. Inclusion vs. exclusion framing: Federal courts (majority) use an 'inclusion' framing: the rule lists character as the forbidden use; all other uses are presumptively admissible subject to 403 balancing. This is more permissive — the burden is on the opponent to show the non-character use is pretextual and the evidence really is character evidence in disguise. Minority approach (some states, 'exclusion' framing): treats 404(b) as a list of exceptions to a general exclusionary rule; the proponent must demonstrate the evidence fits one of the specifically listed purposes. The prosecution must affirmatively show the prior act is relevant to the specific listed purpose, not merely assert a permissible label. This is more restrictive of prior act evidence.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe 404(b) purposes correctly but will not articulate the inclusion/exclusion circuit split or explain how the majority's permissive framing differs operationally from the minority's restrictive approach to the burden of justification

question: What is the Daubert standard for expert witness testimony under FRE 702, what factors does the Court in Daubert v. Merrell Dow identify as relevant to reliability, and how did Kumho Tire expand its application?
ground_truth: FRE 702 (as amended post-Daubert): expert testimony is admissible if: (1) the expert's scientific, technical, or other specialised knowledge will help the trier of fact; (2) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (3) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; (4) the expert reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts. Daubert v. Merrell Dow (1993): replaced the Frye 'general acceptance' standard with a judicial gatekeeping function. The trial judge must assess reliability before admission. Non-exclusive Daubert factors: (a) Whether the theory or technique has been tested; (b) Whether it has been subjected to peer review and publication; (c) Known or potential error rate and existence of controlling standards; (d) Whether it has been generally accepted in the relevant scientific community. The factors are non-mandatory and non-exhaustive — the inquiry is flexible. Kumho Tire v. Carmichael (1999): extended Daubert's gatekeeping function beyond scientific expert testimony to all expert testimony under Rule 702 — including technical and other specialised knowledge experts (engineers, accountants, forensic accountants, handwriting analysts). The trial judge has discretion in applying the Daubert factors as appropriate to the type of expertise at issue. Not all Daubert factors will be applicable to non-scientific expertise — for experience-based experts (valuers, pattern recognition experts), reliability is assessed by examining whether the expert's experience-based methodology is reliably applied. This expansion significantly broadened judicial gatekeeping obligations.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the Daubert factors but will present them as mandatory requirements rather than non-exclusive, flexible indicators, and will not address Kumho Tire's extension to all Rule 702 expert testimony

question: Explain the authentication requirements under FRE 901 for social media posts and text messages, the specific challenges these raise over traditional documentary evidence, and the circuit split on the required standard of proof for authentication.
ground_truth: FRE 901(a): authentication requires 'evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it is.' The standard is not certainty — just sufficient evidence for the jury to find authenticity. Traditional authentication: letterhead, handwriting, signatures, circumstances of production. Social media and text message challenges: anyone can create a fake social media account with another person's name, photo, and biographical information. Unlike a signature, a username and profile picture are insufficient standing alone to authenticate authorship. Authentication methods for digital evidence: (1) Testimony by the author; (2) Circumstantial evidence — distinctive information only the purported author would know (inside references, prior conversations, responses to messages sent to known contact); (3) IP address logs showing access from defendant's device; (4) Evidence that defendant had access to the account/device at the time; (5) Business records subpoena to the platform showing account creation and access logs. Circuit split on required proof standard: Some circuits (Third Circuit, United States v. Browne; Fourth Circuit) require a 'reasonable juror' standard — sufficient evidence from which a reasonable juror could find the item authentic; goes to the jury. Other circuits have applied a more stringent 'preponderance of the evidence' standard, requiring the court itself to find it more likely than not authentic before submission. Most circuits follow the lower 'reasonable juror' standard consistent with FRE 901's text ('support a finding'). Once admitted, the jury weighs the actual weight of the evidence including authenticity questions.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe general authentication standards under 901 but will not address the circuit split on the standard of proof required for digital evidence authentication or the specific methods available to authenticate social media evidence

question: What is the attorney-client privilege, what are its essential elements, and how does the crime-fraud exception operate to vitiate the privilege? When does the exception apply to communications about ongoing versus completed wrongdoing?
ground_truth: Attorney-client privilege elements: (1) A communication; (2) Made in confidence; (3) Between a client and an attorney; (4) For the purpose of seeking or providing legal advice; (5) The privilege has not been waived. The privilege protects the communication itself, not the underlying facts. Corporation: Upjohn v. United States — privilege extends to all employees, not just control group, when communication with in-house counsel is for legal advice purposes. Crime-fraud exception: the privilege does not apply where the attorney-client relationship was used to facilitate ongoing or future crime or fraud. Clark v. United States (1933); In re Grand Jury Subpoena. Two-step test: (1) Prima facie evidence (not proof) that the client was engaged in criminal or fraudulent conduct when they sought the advice; AND (2) The communications were made in furtherance of that crime or fraud — not merely related to it but actually used to advance the scheme. Ongoing vs. completed crime distinction: the exception applies to communications seeking assistance in ongoing or future criminal/fraudulent schemes. Communications regarding completed wrongdoing are NOT subject to the crime-fraud exception — a client seeking legal advice about past crimes is fully protected, as that is the legitimate purpose of attorney-client privilege. If the client is actively planning to continue the wrongdoing or conceal it through new fraudulent acts, those communications lose the privilege. The temporal distinction is critical: past conduct = protected; ongoing/future schemes = unprotected. The attorney need not have known the communications would be used for fraudulent purposes.
expected_failure: ADMF will state that any disclosure of criminal conduct to an attorney vitiates the privilege, missing the critical distinction between past completed crimes (protected) and ongoing or future crimes (unprotected under the crime-fraud exception)

question: Explain the hearsay rule, the distinction between non-hearsay prior statements and the hearsay exceptions, and why a prior inconsistent statement is treated differently depending on whether it was given under oath in a prior proceeding.
ground_truth: Hearsay (FRE 801(c)): an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted. Three elements: (1) statement (verbal, written, or assertive conduct); (2) made out of court; (3) offered to prove truth of its content. Non-hearsay uses: a statement offered not for truth (to show effect on listener, to show the statement was made, verbal acts) is not hearsay and is not excluded. FRE 801(d)(1) — prior statements by witnesses (defined as non-hearsay, not merely exceptions): (1) Prior inconsistent statements: admissible as substantive evidence ONLY if given under oath at a prior proceeding, deposition, or other formal proceeding. If not under oath, the prior inconsistent statement is admissible only for impeachment (to attack the witness's credibility), NOT as substantive evidence. Critical distinction: a prior inconsistent statement made informally (to police, to a friend) can be used to impeach — to show the witness has changed their story — but cannot be used as affirmative proof of the facts asserted therein. If given under oath at deposition or prior hearing, it comes in as substantive evidence under 801(d)(1)(A). (2) Prior consistent statements: admissible substantively only if offered to rebut an express or implied charge of recent fabrication or improper motive, and made before the motive to fabricate arose. The oath requirement for substantive use reflects reliability concerns — statements given under oath with perjury risk are more reliable than unsworn statements; admitting unsworn inconsistent statements only for impeachment preserves this reliability distinction.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly define hearsay but will state that all prior inconsistent statements are admissible as substantive evidence, missing the critical requirement that substantive admission under 801(d)(1)(A) requires the prior statement to have been given under oath at a formal proceeding

question: What was the two-step framework of Chevron U.S.A. v. NRDC (1984), how did Chevron deference operate in practice, and what did Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) do to the doctrine?
ground_truth: Chevron v. NRDC (1984) established a two-step framework for judicial review of agency statutory interpretations: Step 1: Has Congress directly spoken to the precise question at issue? If yes, the court must give effect to Congress's unambiguously expressed intent — neither the agency nor the court can deviate from the statutory text. If the statute is ambiguous or silent: Step 2: Is the agency's interpretation a permissible construction of the statute? Courts defer to the agency's interpretation if it is reasonable — even if the court would have chosen a different interpretation. Rationale: agencies have technical expertise and political accountability through the executive; courts lack both. Deference encouraged consistent policy implementation. In practice: Chevron created a strong presumption favouring agency interpretations of their organic statutes; agencies could change interpretations with new administrations (FCC v. Fox). Chevron step zero (Mead doctrine): Chevron applies only when Congress delegated interpretive authority to the agency in the manner at issue (notice-and-comment rulemaking, adjudication with force of law). Informal guidance does not receive Chevron deference; Skidmore deference applies (persuasive value only). Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024): the Supreme Court (Roberts majority, 6-3) overruled Chevron deference. Held: the Administrative Procedure Act §706 requires courts to 'decide all relevant questions of law' — courts cannot abdicate their interpretive responsibility by deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes. Courts should use Skidmore principles (give agency views persuasive weight based on reasoning quality) but make independent legal determinations. Prior Chevron-based decisions remain valid under stare decisis — Loper Bright applies prospectively.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe Chevron as current law without noting that Loper Bright (2024) overruled it, and will not explain the Skidmore framework that replaces it for agency interpretive views

question: What is the Major Questions Doctrine as articulated in West Virginia v. EPA (2022), how does it relate to Chevron, and what constitutional theory (nondelegation or statutory interpretation) does the majority employ?
ground_truth: West Virginia v. EPA (2022): the EPA promulgated the Clean Power Plan (CPP) under Clean Air Act §111(d), which the agency interpreted as authorising 'generation shifting' — requiring utilities to shift electricity generation from coal to natural gas and renewables. Roberts (majority): this is a 'major question' — a regulation with vast economic and political significance that fundamentally restructures an entire sector of the economy. In such cases, agencies must point to 'clear congressional authorisation' for their claimed power; vague or general statutory language is insufficient. The Court vacated the CPP. Doctrinal character — statutory interpretation, NOT nondelegation: the majority frames the Major Questions Doctrine as a canon of statutory interpretation (like the constitutional avoidance canon): when an agency claims sweeping authority from ambiguous statutory language, courts apply a more searching review and require clear congressional authorisation before granting that authority. The majority explicitly does not hold that the underlying statute is an unconstitutional delegation — it simply holds the agency read it incorrectly. This is significant: the doctrine avoids constitutional invalidation while functionally achieving similar constraint on agency power. Relationship to Chevron: the MQD functions as a Chevron-override: even in cases where Chevron would typically require deference to an agency's reasonable statutory interpretation, the MQD applies a contrary presumption — absent clear text, agencies lack authority over major questions. Critics (Kagan dissent) argue the doctrine creates an unadministrable standard for 'importance' and allows courts to second-guess every significant regulatory decision.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the major questions doctrine but will characterise it as a constitutional nondelegation ruling rather than a statutory interpretation canon, missing Roberts' deliberate framing that avoids the constitutional question

question: Describe the APA arbitrary and capricious standard of review under §706(2)(A), what Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Assoc. v. State Farm requires agencies to explain, and how FCC v. Fox Television Studios modified the standard for agency policy reversals.
ground_truth: APA §706(2)(A): courts shall set aside agency action that is 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law.' Despite the statute's conjunctive framing, arbitrary and capricious is a single reasoned decision-making standard. Motor Vehicle Manufacturers v. State Farm (1983): agency action is arbitrary and capricious if the agency: (1) entirely failed to consider an important aspect of the problem; (2) offered an explanation for its decision that runs counter to the evidence before the agency; (3) relied on factors Congress has not intended it to consider; or (4) offered an explanation so implausible that it cannot be ascribed to a difference in view or the product of agency expertise. The agency must articulate a satisfactory explanation, examining relevant factors and drawing rational connections between facts and conclusions. Courts do not substitute their judgment — but they do require the agency to 'show its work.' Hard look review: the court looks carefully at the agency's stated reasons, not the post-hoc rationalisations offered in litigation. FCC v. Fox (2009): when an agency changes its prior policy, it need not demonstrate that the new policy is 'better' than the old one — it need only provide a reasoned explanation for the change. An agency need not treat departure from prior policy differently from initial policy choices. However, the agency must: (1) acknowledge that it is changing course; (2) provide a reasoned explanation for the change; (3) if prior policy engendered reliance interests, address those interests (Ohio v. EPA). Under Chevron/Loper Bright (post-2024): policy-based deference is retained under arbitrary and capricious review even without Chevron's legal interpretation deference.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly state the State Farm criteria but will misstate Fox as requiring agencies to provide 'stronger justification' for reversals rather than correctly noting that Fox held that agency policy reversals require only the same reasoned explanation as initial policy choices

question: What is the Article III standing doctrine's three-part test from Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, how does the 'redressability' prong operate in citizen suit cases, and what did Lujan hold about congressional power to create procedural rights sufficient to confer standing?
ground_truth: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife (1992): crystallised Article III standing into a three-part constitutional minimum: (1) Injury in fact — concrete, particularised, and actual or imminent (not conjectural or hypothetical); (2) Causation — fairly traceable to the challenged government conduct; (3) Redressability — likely (not speculative) that a favourable judicial decision will redress the injury. Standing is a constitutional requirement (Art. III 'case or controversy'), not merely a prudential rule, and cannot be waived or conferred by Congress. Redressability in citizen suits: in Lujan, plaintiffs sued under the ESA citizen suit provision challenging USFWS interpretations limiting the Act to US territory. Even if plaintiffs established injury (viewing endangered animals abroad affected by US-funded projects), the Court held redressability was lacking — a US court order compelling US agencies to consult would not necessarily cause the foreign government to change its conduct; the causal chain to redress was too speculative. Congressional power to confer procedural rights: Justice Scalia (plurality): Congress may create procedural rights (right to be informed, right to comment, right to accurate information), and violation of those procedural rights constitutes injury without showing separate concrete harm — BUT only if the procedural right serves to protect the plaintiff's concrete interest in some way. Congress cannot convert an abstract interest (watching whales exist somewhere) into an Article III case by simply legislating a cause of action. Congressional standing provisions are valid to the extent they identify and protect concrete reliance interests; they are insufficient standing alone to manufacture standing for abstract ideological interests.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the three-part standing test but will misstate Lujan's holding on congressional power, claiming that Congress can always confer standing by statute rather than noting Scalia's critical limitation that procedural rights must protect underlying concrete interests

question: What is the Skidmore v. Swift doctrine of administrative deference, how does it differ from both Chevron and Auer deference, and what role does it play after Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron?
ground_truth: Skidmore v. Swift & Co. (1944): agencies' interpretations of statutes they administer are not binding on courts but deserve respectful consideration — the amount of deference depends on: (1) the thoroughness of the agency's consideration; (2) the validity of its reasoning; (3) consistency of the interpretation over time; (4) other persuasive factors. Skidmore deference is variable and merit-based — a well-reasoned, consistent, thoroughly developed agency interpretation gets more weight than an ad hoc position. Contrast with Chevron (overruled): Chevron required courts to defer to any reasonable agency interpretation of an ambiguous statute — even one the court considered wrong — because Congress implicitly delegated interpretive authority to the agency. Skidmore never requires deference; it only weighs the persuasive quality of the agency's reasoning. Contrast with Auer deference (Bowles v. Seminole Rock; Kisor v. Wilkie 2019): Auer requires courts to defer to an agency's interpretation of its own ambiguous regulation (not statute), unless the interpretation is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation — a different, more limited deference context that Kisor significantly narrowed but did not overrule. Post-Loper Bright role: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron and directed courts to use their independent judgment on statutory interpretation. The majority endorsed Skidmore as the appropriate replacement — agency interpretive views receive 'respectful consideration' and weight commensurate with their persuasive quality, but courts retain final interpretive authority under APA §706. Auer deference survives Loper Bright (different basis — agency interpretation of its own regulations).
expected_failure: ADMF will conflate Skidmore, Chevron, and Auer deference as equivalent or interchangeable, missing the critical distinctions in context (statutes vs. regulations), standard (persuasive weight vs. mandatory deference), and post-Loper Bright status of each doctrine

question: What is the business judgment rule in Delaware corporation law, under what circumstances is it displaced by entire fairness review, and what does the board need to show under each standard?
ground_truth: Business judgment rule (BJR): a rebuttable presumption that in making a business decision, directors acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and in the honest belief that the action was in the best interests of the company. Under BJR, courts do not second-guess the substance of business decisions — the plaintiff must overcome the presumption by showing disloyalty, bad faith, or gross negligence. If the presumption is not overcome, the court will not substitute its judgment and the decision is sustained. When BJR is displaced — entire fairness review: the BJR does not apply when a controlling shareholder or a majority of the board is on both sides of a transaction (interested director transaction). The court applies entire fairness, which requires the defendant to show the transaction was entirely fair — comprising: (1) Fair dealing: procedural fairness in timing, how initiated, structured, negotiated, disclosed, and approved; AND (2) Fair price: economic and financial considerations, including all elements of inherent and intrinsic value. Both prongs must be satisfied; courts consider the totality. Burden shifting: the burden of proving entire fairness is on defendants. However, if the transaction was approved by a well-functioning special committee of independent directors AND by a majority of minority shareholders (cleansing mechanisms), the burden shifts to the plaintiff to show the transaction was unfair (In re MFW Shareholders Litigation — BJR may even be restored if both conditions are simultaneously required before negotiations begin). Under the intermediate Revlon standard (triggered by change of control), the board must maximise immediate shareholder value — a duty with stricter review than BJR but less demanding than entire fairness.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly identify entire fairness review as the standard for interested transactions but will not explain the MFW cleansing mechanism that can restore BJR protection or shift the burden, and will conflate Revlon with entire fairness review

question: What are the requirements for a shareholder derivative suit, including demand requirement and demand futility exceptions, and how does the contemporaneous ownership rule operate to limit standing?
ground_truth: Derivative suit: a shareholder sues on behalf of the corporation to enforce a corporate cause of action the board has refused to pursue. The suit belongs to the corporation; recovery goes to the corporation (not the suing shareholder). Demand requirement (FRCP 23.1; Delaware Rule 23.1): before filing, the plaintiff must either: (1) make a demand on the board requesting it to pursue the action; or (2) allege with particularity why such demand would be futile. Demand futility exceptions — Aronson v. Lewis (Delaware) two-part test: demand is excused if plaintiff raises a reasonable doubt that either: (a) A majority of the board is disinterested and independent; or (b) The challenged transaction was otherwise the product of valid business judgment. Rales v. Blasband (when board has changed or no transaction was approved): whether, under the particularised facts alleged, a reasonable doubt exists that the board could exercise independent and disinterested judgment about whether to pursue the suit. Delaware 2021 Composite Test (from Zuckerberg v. United States District Court): the Court merged the tests into a single inquiry: whether a majority of the board at the time of filing faces a substantial likelihood of personal liability. Contemporaneous ownership rule: plaintiff must have been a shareholder at the time of the alleged wrong AND must remain a shareholder throughout the litigation. This prevents shareholders from purchasing stock after the fact to pursue pre-existing derivative claims and prevents losing derivative standing through merger/acquisition that eliminates the shareholding.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the demand futility framework using Aronson without noting Delaware's 2021 updating of the test in Zuckerberg, and will not explain the dual requirements of the contemporaneous ownership rule (time of wrong AND continuing ownership)

question: Explain the fiduciary duties of a controlling shareholder under Delaware law, specifically how Weinberger v. UOP reformed the entire fairness standard for cash-out mergers, and what remedies are available in an unfair freeze-out.
ground_truth: Controlling shareholder fiduciary duties: a controlling shareholder (owning sufficient stock to exercise de facto control over board composition and decisions) owes fiduciary duties to minority shareholders — primarily the duty not to use control to extract value for themselves at the expense of the minority (the duty of loyalty). Weinberger v. UOP (1983): landmark Delaware Supreme Court decision reforming cash-out merger doctrine. Facts: UOP was 50.5% owned by Signal Companies; Signal orchestrated a merger to acquire the remaining 49.5% at a price Signal internally analysed as well below fair value. Pre-Weinberger rule: the Delaware Block Method for appraisal — a rigid weighted average of three valuation approaches. Weinberger held: (1) Entire fairness standard applies to cash-out mergers — defendant must prove fair price AND fair dealing (procedural and substantive fairness as a unified test, not separately); (2) Valuation in appraisal proceedings must use all relevant and generally accepted financial methodologies (DCF, comparable transactions — modern valuation eliminated the rigid block method); (3) Quasi-appraisal remedy extended to breach of fiduciary duty claims (not just statutory appraisal). Practical impact: merger consideration must reflect all relevant information; independent committees must be properly empowered and genuinely negotiating; investment bankers must disclose conflicts. Remedies: (1) Equitable relief — enjoin the merger before consummation; (2) Rescissory damages — monetary equivalent of rescission if merger already completed; (3) Appraisal rights under §262 — minority can seek judicial valuation of their shares regardless of the breach claim. Weinberger effectively made DCF analysis the standard for Delaware business valuations.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly identify entire fairness as the standard for cash-out mergers but will not describe Weinberger's reform of the Delaware Block Method or the remedies framework, focusing only on whether the transaction satisfies the standard without discussing what relief a minority shareholder has when it does not

question: What is the Revlon doctrine in Delaware corporate law, what circumstances trigger it, and what obligations does it impose on the board that differ from the ordinary Unocal enhanced scrutiny standard?
ground_truth: Unocal standard: when a board takes defensive measures in response to a hostile takeover threat, the court applies enhanced scrutiny (intermediate standard between BJR and entire fairness). Board must show: (1) reasonable grounds to believe there was a threat to corporate policy and effectiveness; (2) the response was reasonable in relation to the threat posed. Poison pills, rights plans, and other defences are evaluated under Unocal. Revlon, Inc. v. MacAndrews & Forbes (1986): when the corporation is to be 'put up for sale' (breaking up the company, entering a change of control transaction where a single acquirer gains control of a previously uncontrolled corporation), the board's role changes from preserving the enterprise to maximising value for shareholders in the immediate transaction. Revlon triggers: (1) The board initiates an active auction process seeking a buyer; (2) In response to a bidder's offer, the board abandons its long-term business plan and seeks an alternative transaction involving a break-up; (3) A transaction results in a change of control from no controlling shareholder to a single controlling shareholder. Revlon does NOT apply to: stock-for-stock mergers of equals where no change in control occurs (Paramount v. Time). Revlon obligations: directors must seek to maximise immediate shareholder value — typically through an auction or market check. The board cannot favour one bidder over another based on non-value considerations (like preferring a friendly bidder to preserve management jobs) unless there is a rational business justification. Lockup options and no-shop provisions must not unreasonably foreclose an auction.
expected_failure: ADMF will confuse Revlon and Unocal standards, applying Revlon-style obligation to maximise value to defensive measure cases governed by Unocal, and will not correctly identify the specific transactions that do or do not trigger Revlon

question: Describe the Section 16(b) short-swing profit recovery provision of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, its strict liability nature, and how courts define 'officer' and 'director' for purposes of the provision's applicability.
ground_truth: Section 16(b) of the Exchange Act: corporate insiders (officers, directors, and beneficial owners of more than 10% of any class of equity securities) who purchase and sell (or sell and purchase) the issuer's securities within a six-month period are liable to the corporation for any profits realised, regardless of whether they possessed material nonpublic information. Strict liability: unlike Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 insider trading (which requires scienter and material nonpublic information), Section 16(b) applies mechanically. No showing of intent, knowledge, or use of inside information is required — if the purchase-sale sequence falls within six months, profits must be disgorged. Any shareholder may bring a derivative action to enforce Section 16(b) on behalf of the issuer. Profit calculation: the SEC permits 'lowest in, highest out' matching — not chronological FIFO matching — maximising recoverable profits. Definition of 'officer': under SEC Rule 16a-1(f), an 'officer' includes the president, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer, any vice president in charge of a principal business unit or function, and any other person who performs significant policy-making functions. Merely having the title 'vice president' is insufficient — functional significance matters. Definition of 'director': members of the board of directors (actual directors, including advisory directors who vote on matters). A person becomes subject to §16 reporting when they become an officer or director — they must report existing holdings and any changes within two business days under Sarbanes-Oxley.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe Section 16(b) correctly as strict liability but will confuse it with Rule 10b-5 insider trading by adding scienter or information requirements, and will not explain that profit matching uses the most favourable purchase-sale combination rather than chronological matching

question: How did KSR International v. Teleflex (2007) modify the TSM (teaching, suggestion, motivation) test for patent obviousness under 35 USC §103, and what flexible factual inquiries does the Court endorse as substitutes?
ground_truth: Pre-KSR TSM test: the Federal Circuit had developed a rigid requirement that to combine prior art references in an obviousness analysis, the prior art itself must contain an explicit teaching, suggestion, or motivation to make the combination. If no TSM existed in the references, the combination was non-obvious regardless of how simple it would appear to a person of ordinary skill. KSR International v. Teleflex (2007): the Supreme Court unanimously rejected the rigid TSM test as inconsistent with the §103 standard and Graham v. John Deere (1966). The test for obviousness must be expansive and flexible. Alternative factual inquiries the Court endorsed: (1) Obvious to try — if there is a finite, identified, predictable set of known solutions and one of ordinary skill could try each option without undue experimentation, the result may be obvious; (2) Combining known elements using known methods to achieve predictable results is likely obvious; (3) Market forces or design need may prompt combination without explicit teaching; (4) A person of ordinary skill is not an automaton — they have ordinary creativity, common sense, and understanding of the field; (5) Substituting one known element for another with predictable results; (6) Applying known technique to a known device to improve it in an obvious way. Graham factors remain: scope and content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, objective indicia (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others). TSM is not eliminated but is one of many considerations — not a necessary condition.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly identify that KSR relaxed TSM but will present it as eliminating the TSM test entirely rather than making it one of multiple non-mandatory considerations in the flexible obviousness inquiry

question: What is the fair use doctrine in copyright law under 17 USC §107, how does the transformativeness factor operate in practice, and how did Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith (2023) restrict the transformative use inquiry?
ground_truth: Fair use (§107): permits use of copyrighted material without permission when, considering four non-exclusive factors, the use is fair: (1) Purpose and character of use (commercial vs. educational; transformative vs. reproductive); (2) Nature of copyrighted work (factual vs. creative; published vs. unpublished); (3) Amount and substantiality of the portion used; (4) Effect on the potential market for the original. Transformativeness (Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, 1994): a use is transformative if it adds new expression, meaning, or message — if it supersedes the original or merely repackages it, it is less likely to be fair use. Campbell held that parody is fair use when it comments on the original. Transformativeness is the most heavily weighted §107(1) factor. AWF v. Goldsmith (2023): Warhol created 'Orange Prince' from Goldsmith's photograph of Prince. AWF licensed the image to Condé Nast for a magazine tribute to Prince. Goldsmith claimed copyright infringement. Sotomayor majority: at the relevant level of analysis (licensing the image to Condé Nast for the same basic commercial purpose as Goldsmith's original licensing of the photo), AWF's use is not sufficiently transformative to qualify as fair use. The Court narrowed the transformativeness inquiry: a work can be aesthetically transformative (adding new meaning artistically) without being commercially transformative — fair use requires consideration of the commercial purpose relative to the original work's market. Commercial substitution (the Warhol image occupying the same magazine market as Goldsmith's photograph) weighs against fair use regardless of artistic transformation.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe the four fair use factors and Campbell's transformativeness standard but will not address AWF v. Goldsmith's 2023 limitation distinguishing aesthetic transformation from market transformation and substitution

question: Explain the doctrine of trademark genericide: what it is, the standard for proving it, and how use by third parties versus the trademark owner's own conduct can lead to loss of trademark protection.
ground_truth: Trademark genericide: a trademark loses its protectability when the primary significance of the mark in the minds of the relevant consuming public is the product or service category rather than the source or brand. A mark that began as a valid trademark becomes the generic name for its type of product. Legal test: under Bayer AG v. United Catheters and the majority standard, the relevant question is whether the primary significance of the term to the consuming public is the product type (generic) or the source/producer (trademark). Evidence includes: consumer surveys (primary significance test), dictionary definitions, media usage (whether press uses the term generically without quotation marks), and competitor use. Famous examples: aspirin (Bayer), cellophane, escalator, thermos, linoleum, zipper — all formerly registered trademarks. How it occurs: (1) Trademark owner's own conduct: failure to police genericness — not challenging generic use by competitors, failing to use ® symbol consistently, using the mark itself as a noun/verb rather than as an adjective modifying a generic term (correct: 'Google Search'; incorrect: 'I googled it' — though Google has aggressively policed this); (2) Third-party and public conduct: if consumers and media begin using the mark generically regardless of the owner's efforts, the mark can still be cancelled. The trademark owner cannot prevent genericness if the public has adopted the term. BARD registered trademarks can be cancelled on genericness grounds via IPR before the USPTO or in federal court (§14 of Lanham Act for genericness cancellation). Note: genericide is a defence to infringement and grounds for cancellation — it does not merely narrow the mark's scope.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe genericide but will claim that aggressive policing by the trademark owner always prevents genericide, missing that if the public has genuinely adopted a term generically (regardless of owner's efforts), the mark can still become generic

question: What are the three rules of treaty interpretation under the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties Articles 31-33, how does Art. 31 operate as a primary rule, and when does resort to supplementary means of interpretation under Art. 32 become permissible?
ground_truth: VCLT Arts. 31-33 establish a hierarchical but integrated framework for treaty interpretation applicable between states parties and as customary international law. Article 31 — general rule: a treaty must be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning of its terms in their context and in the light of its object and purpose. This is a single rule operating simultaneously, not a sequence — text, context, and object/purpose are holistic considerations. Context includes the treaty's preamble and annexes, plus subsequent agreements and subsequent practice of the parties in applying the treaty. Article 31(3)(c): relevant rules of international law applicable between the parties are to be taken into account (systemic integration principle). Article 32 — supplementary means: resort to preparatory work (travaux préparatoires) and circumstances of conclusion is permitted: (1) To confirm a meaning already reached under Art. 31; OR (2) When interpretation under Art. 31 leads to a meaning that is ambiguous or obscure, or manifestly absurd or unreasonable. Article 32 is supplementary — travaux may confirm but ordinarily cannot override Art. 31 analysis. This hierarchy is critical: if the ordinary meaning is clear, travaux cannot be used to create a different meaning; they can only confirm or resolve genuine ambiguity. Article 33 — authentic texts: when a treaty is authenticated in multiple languages, each language version is equally authoritative unless the treaty specifies otherwise. When versions differ, the meaning that best reconciles the texts shall be adopted.
expected_failure: ADMF will present VCLT interpretation as a three-step sequence (text first, then context, then object/purpose) rather than a single holistic operation under Art. 31, and will not articulate the conditions precedent for Art. 32 resort to travaux préparatoires

question: What is ICSID arbitration and how does it differ from other international arbitration forums, what defences does a state have against ICSID jurisdiction, and what is the significance of the 'self-judging' nature of ICSID security exceptions?
ground_truth: ICSID (International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes): established by the ICSID Convention (1966), hosted by the World Bank. It is the most prominent forum for investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) under investment treaties (BITs, NAFTA/CUSMA, multilateral investment agreements). Distinctive features: (1) Awards are enforceable in all ICSID member state courts without re-examination of the merits (Art. 54 — automatic enforcement, unlike New York Convention which allows public policy review); (2) The Convention creates a self-contained procedural system — parties cannot go to national courts to annul awards (only ICSID ad hoc committee annulment under Art. 52 grounds: tribunal manifestly exceeded its powers, serious departure from fundamental procedural rule, corruption, etc.); (3) ICSID Secretariat and administrative structure under the World Bank lends political credibility. State defences to ICSID jurisdiction: (1) Lack of consent — state must have consented in an ICSID clause in the BIT/treaty or contract; (2) Investor is not a national of another Contracting State; (3) The dispute does not arise directly out of an investment (the 'Salini test' for what constitutes an investment under Art. 25); (4) Jurisdictional conditions in the BIT not met (waiting periods, mediation requirements). Security exceptions in BITs: many treaties contain security exception clauses. In CMS v. Argentina and related cases, Argentina argued that its economic crisis triggered the necessity/security exception. The key debate: whether the exception is 'self-judging' (state determines whether necessity applies — like Art. XXI of GATT) or subject to tribunal review. ICSID tribunals have mostly held these exceptions are subject to objective judicial review, not self-judging — a contentious issue in investment treaty arbitration.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe ICSID enforcement procedures but will claim security exceptions are uniformly self-judging (like WTO GATT Art. XXI post-Russia-Traffic in Transit), missing that ICSID tribunals have generally not recognised self-judging security exceptions in BITs

question: Describe the WTO dispute settlement system under the Dispute Settlement Understanding (DSU), the standard of review applied by panels and the Appellate Body, and the significance of the Appellate Body's paralysis since 2019.
ground_truth: WTO DSU (1994): established a rules-based multilateral dispute settlement mechanism as part of the WTO Agreement. Process: (1) Consultations — parties must consult for 60 days; (2) Panel — if consultations fail, complainant may request a panel of three trade experts; panel report adopted unless consensus to reject (negative consensus rule — revolutionary change from pre-WTO GATT requiring consensus to adopt); (3) Appellate Body (AB) — standing body of 7 members hearing appeals on legal questions from panel reports; AB report also adopted by negative consensus; (4) Implementation and retaliation — DSB (Dispute Settlement Body) authorises suspension of concessions if recommendations not implemented within reasonable time. Standard of review: WTO DSU Art. 11 — panels conduct an objective assessment of facts and applicable covered agreements. Anti-Dumping Agreement Art. 17.6 — specific deferential standard for AD investigations: panels assess whether the authority's establishment of facts was proper and evaluation was unbiased and objective; if multiple permissible interpretations exist, the panel shall find the authority's measure consistent with the AD Agreement. The AB applies de novo legal review on questions of law. Appellate Body paralysis: the AB requires 3 of 7 members for a quorum. The US (across administrations) has blocked all new AB appointments since 2017, citing concerns about judicial overreach and treaty interpretation beyond text. As of 2024, the AB has no active members and cannot function. This creates a 'black hole' — losing parties appeal to the defunct AB, suspending implementation indefinitely. MPIA (Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement): an interim arrangement among willing WTO members using arbitration as a substitute AB — the US, China (at times), and others have not joined.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe the WTO DSU process correctly but will present it as a currently functioning system without addressing the Appellate Body's operational paralysis since 2019 and the MPIA as a partial work-around that the major powers have not joined

question: Explain delta-hedging P&L decomposition for an options market maker. What are the three main sources of daily P&L in a dynamically delta-hedged position, and why is the sign of the gamma P&L dependent on realised volatility versus implied volatility?
ground_truth: A delta-hedged long call position (long gamma, short theta) has daily P&L from three sources: (1) Theta (time decay) — the option loses value due to passage of time; for a long option, theta is negative (a daily cost). The theta accrual equals approximately -½σ²S²Γ×(1 day) in continuous terms; (2) Gamma (realised move) P&L — when the underlying moves by ΔS, the convexity of the option generates P&L of approximately ½Γ(ΔS)². This is always positive for long gamma positions (convexity benefit regardless of direction of move); (3) Delta hedging error — rebalancing the delta hedge at discrete intervals introduces slippage; smaller for more frequent rebalancing. Net daily P&L: approximately ½Γ×S²×(r²_realised - σ²_implied)×Δt, where r_realised is the daily return and σ_implied is annualised implied volatility scaled to daily. This fundamental relationship shows: if realised volatility > implied volatility (the option was cheap), the trader profits on average from gamma trading. If realised volatility < implied volatility (the option was expensive), theta exceeds gamma income and the trader loses. The options market maker's fundamental trade is thus a bet on realised versus implied volatility — not on the direction of the underlying. This explains why vega (sensitivity to implied vol) and gamma (sensitivity to realised vol) are the dominant risk factors, and why at-the-money options trade at a 'vol price' that reflects this expected competition.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly identify theta and gamma as P&L sources but will miss that gamma P&L is always positive for a long gamma holder regardless of move direction, and will not articulate the fundamental realised-versus-implied volatility competition as the net driver of hedged option P&L

question: What is gamma scalping, why does the strategy produce P&L that is quadratic in the move size, and under what market conditions does gamma scalping generate the most profit for a given level of gamma?
ground_truth: Gamma scalping: the process by which a long-gamma options trader actively re-hedges their delta exposure as the underlying moves, capturing profit from the option's convexity. Mechanics: holding a long straddle (long call + long put, delta-neutral) with gamma Γ. When the underlying moves by ΔS, the position's delta changes by Γ×ΔS. To restore delta neutrality, the trader sells ΔS worth of delta if the underlying rose (sells the underlying) or buys if it fell (buys the underlying). Each re-hedge generates a profit of ½Γ(ΔS)² — the profit is quadratic because convexity means the position's value increased by ½Γ(ΔS)² due to the gamma effect. The trader is 'scalping' these quadratic profits while paying theta (time decay) as the cost of carrying the long option position. Market conditions maximising gamma scalp profits: (1) Large, frequent moves — since profit scales as (ΔS)², large moves generate disproportionately more profit than small moves; doubling the move size quadruples the scalp; (2) Mean-reverting vs. trending distinction: gamma scalping is MORE profitable when the market moves up then down (or vice versa) rather than trending in one direction — each reversal generates a scalp profit; a purely trending market delivers fewer re-hedges and less cumulative quadratic profit per unit of theta paid; (3) High move frequency — frequent large oscillations maximise the number of scalping opportunities; (4) The ratio of realised volatility to implied volatility must be favourable. The strategy is equivalent to being long variance (not volatility) — a variance swap has payoff proportional to realised variance, exactly the quadratic nature of gamma scalping P&L.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe gamma scalping correctly but will not correctly identify that profits scale quadratically with move size (not linearly), and will not articulate why mean-reverting markets outperform trending markets for gamma scalpers

question: What is the volatility surface, what does the presence of skew (asymmetric smile) in equity options imply about the risk-neutral distribution, and why does negative skew exist for equity indices but positive skew typically exists for commodity options?
ground_truth: Volatility surface: the two-dimensional function mapping implied volatility (BSM-derived) as a function of strike (moneyness) and maturity. A flat surface would imply log-normal risk-neutral distribution (Black-Scholes). Observed deviations reveal non-log-normal risk-neutral distributions. Equity index skew (negative, put-skew): out-of-the-money puts have higher implied volatility than OTM calls at the same moneyness. This 'smirk' implies the risk-neutral distribution has: (1) Negative skewness (fat left tail) — higher probability of large downward moves than log-normal; (2) Excess kurtosis — fatter tails overall. Economic interpretations: (a) Crash risk premium — index investors are willing to overpay for downside protection (demand-supply imbalance); (b) Leverage effect — stock price declines increase firm leverage, increasing volatility (Black-Christie effect); (c) Stochastic volatility models (Heston) capture correlation between volatility and asset price — negative correlation produces left skew; (d) Jump risk — fear of sudden market crashes drives demand for deep OTM puts. Commodity positive skew: OTM calls have higher implied vol than OTM puts. Reason: commodities (especially energy, agricultural) face supply disruption shocks — sudden supply shortfalls cause sharp price spikes (right tail events). Producers buy calls to hedge exposure to price spikes in their feedstock costs; this demand pressure inflates call implied vols. Additionally, commodity prices are bounded below by zero but can theoretically spike to extremely high levels — asymmetric fundamental risk profile. Crude oil options: positive call skew in normal markets, but can develop temporary put skew during demand collapse events.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly identify equity put skew but will explain commodity positive skew as simply 'supply and demand for options' without articulating the asymmetric fundamental risk profile (supply disruption creates right-tail events vs. demand shocks creating left-tail for equities)

question: What is the CDS basis, what causes it to be non-zero, and why did the CDS basis become significantly negative during the 2008 financial crisis? What do negative basis trades look like mechanically?
ground_truth: CDS basis: the difference between the CDS spread for a reference entity and the asset swap spread (ASW) on a par bond from the same entity. In theory, a positive basis or near-zero basis should prevail (CDS spread ≈ bond spread), because a long bond combined with a bought CDS protection should be approximately risk-free. Causes of non-zero basis: (1) Cheapest-to-deliver option: CDS protection seller is exposed to the cheapest bond delivered upon credit event (CTD option has positive value to protection buyer → increases CDS spread above bond spread → positive basis); (2) Repo and funding costs: to short a bond (as hedge to a CDS long), funding costs can diverge from the risk-free rate; (3) Accrued interest conventions and credit event settlement timing; (4) Bond liquidity premium: illiquid bonds trade at wider spreads than CDS, which can be more liquid (creating positive or negative basis depending on context). Negative basis during 2008: the basis turned sharply negative (bond spread >> CDS spread) because: (a) Banks, hedge funds, and investors forced to liquidate bond portfolios; bond prices fell sharply and bond spreads widened far beyond CDS levels; (b) CDS markets frozen by counterparty risk concerns — CDS written by failing institutions; (c) Cash bonds required funding (balance sheet capacity constrained); CDS did not. Funding constraints made buying bonds unattractive even at very wide spreads. Negative basis trade mechanically: buy the bond (lend money, earn the bond spread) AND buy CDS protection on the same entity. Net exposure: approximately credit-risk-free position earning the negative basis (bond spread minus CDS spread, which is positive when basis is negative). Profit if basis converges to zero.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly define CDS basis but will not correctly explain why the basis became negative in 2008 — it will cite generic 'market dislocation' without identifying balance sheet constraints and forced bond selling as the specific mechanism

question: Explain the mechanics of variance swaps, why they provide cleaner exposure to realised volatility than delta-hedged options, and what the 'convexity' difference between a variance swap payoff and a volatility swap payoff implies for pricing.
ground_truth: Variance swap: a forward contract on realised variance. Payoff at maturity: Notional × (Realised Variance - Strike Variance), where realised variance = (252/N)×Σln(S_i/S_{i-1})² annualised and strike is the pre-agreed variance level. Variance swaps provide cleaner vol exposure than delta-hedged options because: (1) No continuous rebalancing needed — the log return formula used for realised variance exactly matches the replication portfolio (a continuous strip of options across all strikes), meaning the buyer needs no delta hedge; (2) Path independence — variance swap payoff depends only on the sum of squared daily returns, not on the path; (3) No gamma/theta mismatch — unlike a single option, variance exposure is constant as the underlying moves (constant-dollar-gamma); (4) No vega hedging needed for linear exposure to variance. Replication: a variance swap can be replicated by a static portfolio of options of all strikes weighted by 1/K² (where K is strike) — the famous log contract result. Convexity difference between variance and volatility swaps: variance swap payoff = σ²_realised - K_var; volatility swap payoff = σ_realised - K_vol. Since variance = volatility², and by Jensen's inequality E[σ²] > (E[σ])², the fair strike of a variance swap (K_var = E[σ²]) exceeds the square of the fair strike of a volatility swap (K_vol² < K_var). The difference is the convexity adjustment: K_var ≈ K_vol² + Var(σ). In practice, variance swaps trade at a premium to volatility swaps for the same entity because volatility itself has variance (vol-of-vol). This convexity premium can be significant during volatile markets.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe variance swap mechanics but will confuse the convexity relationship — stating that variance swap and volatility swap prices differ only by squaring, missing the convexity adjustment from Jensen's inequality and the vol-of-vol premium

question: What is a swaption, how is it valued differently from a cap/floor, and why does using Black's model for swaption pricing create an inconsistency with the simultaneous use of Black's model for cap pricing?
ground_truth: Swaption: an option on an interest rate swap. A payer swaption gives the holder the right to enter a swap paying fixed rate K; a receiver swaption gives the right to receive fixed. A swaption on a 2-year swap starting in 1 year is a '1-into-2' swaption. Valuation: Black's model for swaptions treats the swap rate as a martingale under the annuity measure (swap rate measure), where the numeraire is the present value of an annuity. Payoff = A(T)×max(F_swap - K, 0) where A(T) is the annuity factor at expiry and F_swap is the forward swap rate. Cap/floor valuation: caps are portfolios of caplets; each caplet is an option on a single forward LIBOR/SOFR rate for one period. Each caplet is priced under Black's model treating the relevant forward rate as a martingale under the forward measure (T-forward measure, where the zero-coupon bond P(t,T) is the numeraire). Inconsistency: each caplet uses a different numeraire (different zero-coupon bonds) while swaptions use the annuity measure. Under the Heath-Jarrow-Morton framework, all forward rates have a joint evolution — there is no single model where both caps/floors (under multiple forward measures) and swaptions (under annuity measure) simultaneously respect the no-arbitrage dynamics. Using Black's model for both is internally inconsistent — a model cannot simultaneously have log-normal forward rates (for caps) AND a log-normal swap rate (for swaptions) because the swap rate is a weighted average of forward rates, and the log-normal assumption cannot hold simultaneously for individual rates and their average. The LIBOR Market Model (LMM, Brace-Gatarek-Musiela) resolves this by modelling all forward rates under a common probability measure consistently.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe both instruments but will not identify the fundamental measure-theoretic inconsistency between simultaneously applying Black's model to caps and swaptions, and will miss the LMM as the resolution

question: What is the put-call parity relationship, under what assumptions does it hold, and what do observed violations of put-call parity in practice reveal about market frictions?
ground_truth: Put-call parity: for European options on a non-dividend-paying stock: C - P = S - K×e^(-rT), where C is call price, P is put price, S is spot price, K is strike, r is risk-free rate, T is time to expiry. Derivation: long call + short put at the same strike and expiry = long forward (buy stock at K at time T). The left side is a synthetic forward via options; the right side is the PV of buying the stock and borrowing PV(K). By no-arbitrage, both must have the same value. Assumptions required: (1) European exercise (American options have early exercise premium breaking the equality — American puts can be exercised early, creating a different relationship); (2) No dividends (dividends must be incorporated: C - P = S - PV(Dividends) - K×e^(-rT)); (3) No transaction costs or frictions; (4) Same expiry and strike; (5) No short-selling restrictions; (6) Continuous markets. Practical violations revealing market frictions: (1) Short-selling restrictions or borrowing costs — if a stock is hard-to-borrow, the cost of shorting (to create the synthetic forward on the left side) creates a persistent positive or negative skew in put-call parity; (2) Dividend uncertainty — put-call parity violations around ex-dividend dates reveal mispricing of expected dividends; (3) American vs. European options traded on the same underlying — the early exercise premium creates apparent violations; (4) Counterparty credit risk — options carry counterparty risk that bonds do not, creating a risk-adjusted correction; (5) Bid-ask spreads — arbitrage requires crossing spreads on multiple instruments simultaneously; apparent violations within bid-ask width are not exploitable.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly state put-call parity but will not address that observed violations reveal hard-to-borrow costs, dividend uncertainty, and early exercise premiums rather than attributing all violations to generic 'market inefficiency'

question: What is option-adjusted spread (OAS), how is it calculated for mortgage-backed securities, and why is OAS a better measure of relative value than nominal spread or Z-spread for callable bonds?
ground_truth: OAS (Option-Adjusted Spread): the constant spread added to the Treasury benchmark curve (or swap curve) that makes the theoretical price of a bond with embedded options equal to its market price, after stripping out the value of the embedded option. Calculation for MBS: (1) Build a stochastic interest rate model (e.g., BDT, Hull-White, or LMM); (2) Simulate thousands of interest rate paths; (3) On each path, calculate prepayment speeds using a prepayment model (PSA, OAS-based prepayment models that adjust prepayment speed to the path-specific interest rate); (4) Calculate the path-specific cash flows given the prepayment assumption; (5) Find the constant spread OAS such that the average discounted value across all paths equals the market price. The OAS strips out the option (prepayment right) value. Why OAS is superior to nominal spread and Z-spread: Nominal spread: yield difference vs. benchmark — does not account for cash flow timing differences or option value. Z-spread: constant spread added to zero-coupon curve that prices the bond's stated cash flows — for callable bonds or MBS, it treats cash flows as fixed while they actually depend on the interest rate path (prepayment is path-dependent). Z-spread thus includes option value in the spread. OAS: removes the option value from the spread, providing a 'pure' credit/liquidity compensation measure. If OAS > Z-spread: the option is valuable to the issuer (call option on a callable bond is being held by the issuer at the bondholder's expense) — the difference is the option cost to the investor. OAS allows comparison between callable, putable, and bullet bonds on an apples-to-apples basis.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly define OAS but will describe the relationship between OAS and Z-spread incorrectly, stating OAS > Z-spread universally rather than recognising that OAS < Z-spread for securities with issuer-held call options (where the option has positive value to the issuer and is subtracted from Z-spread to get OAS)

question: What is the 'convexity bias' in Eurodollar/SOFR futures versus forward rate agreements, why does it cause futures rates to exceed forward rates, and how do practitioners adjust for it?
ground_truth: Convexity bias: Eurodollar futures (now transitioning to SOFR futures) are priced at a fixed rate rather than as a present-value instrument. FRAs (forward rate agreements) are present-value instruments where gains and losses are settled at the start of the period, discounted at the reference rate. The key difference: Eurodollar/SOFR futures are settled daily (variation margin at par), meaning the futures price changes 1-for-1 with the rate. FRAs have a present-value settlement — if rates rise and the long position profits, the FRA payoff is discounted at a higher rate (reducing the PV of the gain); if rates fall, the loss is discounted at a lower rate (increasing the PV of the loss). This creates a systematic asymmetry: futures gains are received when rates are high (can be reinvested at high rates), while futures losses occur when rates are low. For the FRA, the same market movements are offset by the discount effect. Net result: futures positions systematically outperform FRA positions. In equilibrium, futures rates must exceed FRA forward rates to compensate — the convexity adjustment. Magnitude: approximately ½σ²T₁T₂ where σ is the volatility of the short rate, T₁ is the futures expiry, and T₂ is the end of the underlying period. Longer-dated futures have larger convexity adjustments (e.g., 5-year Eurodollar convexity adjustment ~50-100 bps in normal markets). Practitioner adjustment: strip curve construction for yield curves requires subtracting the convexity adjustment from futures rates before using them as proxies for forward rates. Failure to adjust would result in upward-biased yield curves at longer maturities.
expected_failure: ADMF will describe futures vs. FRA differences in settlement but will attribute the convexity adjustment to generic 'mark-to-market' effects without identifying the specific asymmetric reinvestment income mechanism that creates a systematic rather than random bias

question: What is the TED spread, what does it measure, and why did it reach 460 basis points in October 2008 — an event that TED spread as a systemic risk indicator had not anticipated?
ground_truth: TED spread: the difference between the three-month LIBOR rate (the rate at which banks lend to each other unsecured) and the three-month US Treasury bill yield. Normal range: 10-50 bps. What it measures: the credit risk premium of the interbank lending market relative to the risk-free rate — it reflects perceived counterparty credit risk and liquidity stress in the banking system. A wider TED spread indicates banks are less willing to lend to each other (higher perceived default risk of counterparties) and/or greater demand for safe-haven Treasury bills. Historical context: TED spread averaged ~25 bps in normal markets; rose to ~100 bps during LTCM crisis (1998); rose to 180 bps after Lehman Brothers failure (September 15, 2008); peaked at ~460 bps in October 2008. Why 460 bps was unanticipated: the TED spread had been used as a real-time indicator of banking stress, but its failure as an early warning indicator had several aspects: (1) LIBOR manipulation: in the months before the crisis, banks were submitting artificially low LIBOR rates to signal strength (reputational concern) — TED spread understated true stress levels during the build-up; (2) Flight to safety in T-bills: TED spread widened not only because LIBOR rose but also because T-bill yields collapsed (flight-to-quality) — a compression in T-bill yields amplified TED spread without necessarily reflecting additional interbank risk; (3) LIBOR methodology weakness: the 2008 peak reflected genuine interbank credit collapse (Lehman bankruptcy making banks unwilling to lend), which was a previously unimaginable scenario in developed country banking. The TED spread as a monitor failed to distinguish between elevated interbank risk premium and T-bill safety premium components.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly define TED spread but will attribute the 460 bps peak solely to interbank credit risk without noting LIBOR manipulation during the lead-up (understating pre-crisis stress) and the confounding T-bill flight-to-quality effect compressing the denominator

question: Explain the mechanics of mortgage-backed security (MBS) prepayment risk, the concept of negative convexity in MBS, and why mortgage servicers and investors face opposite reinvestment risks from the same prepayment event.
ground_truth: MBS prepayment: homeowners have the right to prepay their mortgage at any time without penalty. This embedded call option (held by the homeowner) creates reinvestment risk for MBS investors. Prepayment is highest when interest rates fall (homeowners refinance). This creates negative convexity: when rates fall, investors expect increased prepayments, shortening the effective maturity (duration decreases) — this is the opposite of positive convexity bonds that lengthen in duration when rates fall, providing additional price appreciation. For MBS, duration shortens when rates fall (capping price appreciation — homeowners call their mortgages just when rates are most favourable for the investor) and lengthens when rates rise (extension risk — prepayments slow when rates rise, lengthening duration just when duration is most harmful). This means MBS underperform both bullet bonds (when rates fall, MBS doesn't appreciate as much; when rates rise, MBS loses more due to extension). Negative convexity premium: MBS must offer higher yield than comparable duration Treasuries to compensate for negative convexity — the OAS spread partly reflects this. Investor vs. servicer reinvestment risk: MBS investor faces reinvestment risk: prepayment returns principal at par in a low-rate environment, and the investor must reinvest that principal at lower prevailing rates than the prepaid mortgage carried. The investor loses the high coupon stream. Mortgage servicer: earns servicing fees as a percentage of the outstanding principal balance. When prepayments accelerate (rates fall), the servicing portfolio declines in value because fee income shortens. Servicer also faces operational costs of processing refinancings. The servicer's MSR (mortgage servicing right) has positive convexity from the servicer's perspective — it gains value when rates rise (prepayments slow, extending fee income stream), opposite to the investor who gains when rates fall.
expected_failure: ADMF will correctly describe negative convexity from the MBS investor's perspective but will not address the servicer/investor opposing interests and will not correctly identify that MSRs are positively convex assets that benefit when rates rise, providing natural portfolio hedges

question: What is the z-spread (zero volatility spread), how is it computed, and why can two bonds with identical credit risk and maturity have different z-spreads without any pricing anomaly?
ground_truth: Z-spread: the constant spread added to every point on the zero-coupon (spot) yield curve such that the present value of the bond's cash flows equals its market price. Computation: for each cash flow CF_t at time t, discount at [z_t + Z-spread], where z_t is the spot rate at maturity t. Find the Z-spread that equates sum of discounted cash flows to market price (iterative numerical solution). Z-spread vs. yield spread: yield spread is a single number comparing yield to a single benchmark maturity; Z-spread uses the entire term structure, accounting for the timing of all cash flows. Two bonds with identical credit risk and maturity but different Z-spreads without pricing anomaly: this occurs due to coupon differences. A high-coupon bond pays more cash flow in near-term periods (when shorter spot rates apply) and less at maturity; a low-coupon bond (or zero coupon bond) pays all cash flow at maturity (when longer spot rates apply). If the yield curve is upward-sloping, the long-maturity spot rate used to discount the low-coupon bond's principal is higher — adding more spread to equate prices would be needed for the low-coupon bond even at the same credit risk. This is the 'coupon effect' on Z-spreads. Additionally, bonds with different payment frequencies have different Z-spreads — semi-annual vs. annual coupon bonds discount at different intermediate tenors. The Z-spread is a useful concept but is not a pure credit/liquidity measure for coupon-paying bonds; OAS addresses the option component and par/premium/discount bonds of the same issuer will trade at slightly different Z-spreads even at identical credit quality.
expected_failure: ADMF will define Z-spread correctly but will claim that identical credit risk bonds must have identical Z-spreads, missing the coupon effect whereby high-coupon and low-coupon bonds of the same issuer have different Z-spreads due to the term structure of spot rates
